questions.title: What is Online Reputation Monitoring & Brand Mention Tracking?
questions.answer: Online Reputation Monitoring & Brand Mention Tracking — also called online brand monitoring or internet reputation monitoring — is a full-program retainer for enterprise reputation monitoring and media monitoring services: ongoing, real-time monitoring of everything published about you across media, social, search, reviews and AI-generated answers, read by analysts who separate signal from noise and escalate confirmed risk to a team — not a self-serve listening dashboard.

questions.title: How is this different from Control (SERM) or Crisis Management (Defence)?
questions.answer: Continuous Monitoring only watches and signals — it doesn't change your search results (that's RH Control) and it doesn't fight an active crisis (that's RH Defence). Think of it as the layer that tells you when either of those is needed, before it becomes obvious to everyone else.

questions.title: What's included in the five RCC modules?
questions.answer: As part of our reputation monitoring services: search results (SERP), social & mention listening (SCAN), AI answer tracking, reviews & ratings, and sentiment/tone — all five run together as one contour, with a shared RPN risk score and alerting on top.

questions.title: Does this include AI assistants like ChatGPT and Gemini?
questions.answer: Yes. AI Representation Analysis tracks how ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok and Perplexity answer real questions about you, scored on relevance, volume and how clean of negative framing the answer came back.

questions.title: How is pricing structured?
questions.answer: A monthly retainer, $5–25K/month, depending on the scope of your field, languages and regions. Full tiers are on the pricing page, or a confidential audit confirms the exact quote.

questions.title: Is this online media monitoring, or does it cover offline channels too?
questions.answer: This is online brand surveillance and monitoring — media, social, search, reviews and AI answers across digital channels. Broadcast and print aren't covered; if a story breaks there, it almost always surfaces online within hours, and that's where the platform picks it up.

questions.title: Is this a media tracking service, or software I run myself?
questions.answer: It's a media tracking service, not self-serve software. You get full platform access to Risk Control Center, but a dedicated analyst team reads the field every day and escalates confirmed risk — the software alone is what a SaaS monitoring tool sells you.

questions.title: How much media mentions tracking is actually included — every single mention?
questions.answer: Media mentions tracking runs across your entire field — media, social, search, reviews and AI answers — but analysts filter signal from noise first. You're not handed a raw feed of every mention; you see the ones that are actually risk, scored and prioritized.

questions.title: Is this suitable for compliance teams, or just PR/comms?
questions.answer: Yes. For General Counsel and compliance leads, this runs as online brand compliance monitoring — negative-news screening built into ongoing coverage, not a one-off check before a deal. Any media monitoring organization, from a single enterprise brand to a multi-brand holding, gets the same one-score view.

sections.title: What is Social Listening? Quick Definition
body: Social listening is tracking what people say about your brand across social platforms, forums, blogs, video and press, then reading it for tone and risk — not just counting how many times you were mentioned. Social monitoring is the narrower version of that: watching a channel for volume and alerts. Most brands actually want something in between: a social listening platform that also has someone reading it. Whatever you call the category: social listening software or social media monitoring software — that's the version this page describes.

questions.answer: Monitoring usually means watching one channel for volume and basic alerts. What runs on this retainer combines both: full-channel coverage plus a human who actually reads it.

Mass discount codes can drive most of the growth in mentions, while a handful of niche organic placements deliver disproportionately higher engagement per mention.

cards.title: The Sign
parts: ChatGPT gets asked about you, and nobody at your company sees the answer. A customer, investor or candidate asks an AI-powered assistant about your company — the answer could be accurate, outdated or unflattering, and right now you have no way of knowing which.
Why it matters

AI answers are becoming the first impression. For a growing share of buyers, investors and candidates, that answer is the only account of your company they see before they decide. It carries your brand's voice whether you wrote a word of it or not — shaping brand reputation before you know it happened.

cards.title: The Sign
parts: No one owns this yet. SEO owns Google. PR owns the media. Marketing owns the campaigns. Nobody’s job description says "watch what ChatGPT says about us" — so it sits unmanaged in the gap between teams.
Why it matters

The model recommends — someone has to know what it’s recommending. Ask an AI assistant to compare vendors, employers or investment targets and it picks a shortlist. Nobody’s watching whether your company makes that shortlist, or why it doesn’t.

cards.title: The Sign
parts: You’d find out from a customer, a journalist or a screenshot — not from your own team. Nobody is systematically checking what ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity say about you until someone outside the company mentions it.
Why it matters
By the time it’s visible to you, it’s already been visible to everyone it’s going to reach. Early warning only works if someone's actually watching, continuously — not reacting after the fact.

cards.title: The Sign
parts: Nobody’s checked since the last model update. An answer that was fine last quarter can be wrong today, and nothing tells you unless you’re tracking it continuously.
Why it matters

It doesn’t wait for you to catch up. ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity retrain and re-index on their own schedules — so watching this has to be continuous, not a one-time check that ages out with the next release.

cards.title: The Sign
parts: Manual spot-checks catch a fraction of what’s actually being asked. Someone on the team occasionally types a question into ChatGPT — that’s not coverage, it’s a sample of one, on one platform, whenever someone remembers.
Why it matters

Coverage has to mean every platform, every day. ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and Google’s AI Overviews don’t answer the same way about the same company — missing one means missing exactly where the risk actually is.

questions.title: How fast do I get alerted when something changes?
questions.answer: Depends on how each platform re-indexes or retrains — some shifts surface within days, others only at the next major model update. We track this per platform and alert on actual score movement, not a fixed reporting cycle.

questions.title: Is this confidential?

questions.title: How is pricing structured?

questions.title: How does brand monitoring for AI results differ from regular search monitoring?
questions.answer: Regular search monitoring tracks where you rank in a list of blue links. AI results are different — there's no ranking, just one generated answer that either represents you accurately or doesn't. We track the answer itself, across every platform, and flag it the moment it turns wrong.

questions.title: What is brand reputation management?
questions.answer: Brand reputation management — or reputation management for business, if you're searching by outcome rather than category — is the ongoing practice of monitoring, protecting and shaping everything a company's market finds about it: search, reviews, media narrative, sentiment and AI-generated answers.It is the enterprise form of online reputation management, run with an owned narrative, a dedicated team and a measurement framework, rather than reacting to individual results as they appear. At Reputation House it is delivered as Strategic Information-Field Management, RH Control's full-program retainer.

questions.title: What is the difference between ORM and SERM?
questions.answer: SERM covers one surface: what ranks on Google, Bing and YouTube for your brand name. Online reputation management covers all of them, adding reviews, media narrative and AI answers. SERM is a workstream inside this program and also runs as a standalone retainer, as does the narrative and content layer on its own.

questions.title: What are the key strategies for effective reputation management?
questions.answer: A working reputation strategy has four parts, and a reputation management strategy that skips any one of them leaks. Continuous reputation monitoring, so you learn about a problem before your customers do. A content strategy that builds owned assets worth ranking, supported by search engine optimization rather than replaced by it. Structured review management services, so ratings reflect the actual customer base. And a crisis protocol agreed in advance, so the first hour of a bad day is not spent deciding who speaks. Proactive reputation management is cheaper than repair, consistently.

questions.title: How much do reputation management services cost?
questions.answer: Across the market the range runs from a few hundred dollars a month for a review-response tool to five figures a month for a fully managed enterprise program. This one is a monthly retainer, $10–50K/month, scoped to region, channels and the size of your information field rather than listed as a package. Single workstreams are cheaper on their own. Full tiers by region are on the pricing page, and a confidential audit confirms the exact quote.

questions.title: How long does this take to show results?
questions.answer: Monitoring starts immediately, with threat detection inside 24–48 hours. Measurable shifts typically appear in 8–12 weeks, with significant change in 3–6 months, depending on scope.

questions.title: Can you remove negative content or negative search results from Google?
questions.answer: Sometimes. Where content breaches a platform's policy, contains factual errors or infringes a legal right, negative content removal is possible and we pursue it. Where it does not, the honest answer is suppression: we build and rank stronger assets so the harmful result drops down the page. We do not promise to remove negative news articles that are lawful and accurate, and anyone who does is describing something we would not sign.

questions.title: How do you handle negative reviews and negative feedback?
questions.answer: By responding, not by hiding. Every negative review gets a reply written to be read by the next reader rather than by the complainant, since that is who it actually persuades. Underneath that, we track patterns across review sites and social media platforms: repeated customer review themes are usually a product signal, and passing that back is worth more than any individual response. Volume of positive reviews is then built the legitimate way, by asking satisfied customers at the right moment, never by buying them.

questions.title: How does AI change online reputation management?
questions.answer: It changes what counts as page one. Assistants answer directly instead of listing links, so a single stale source can become the whole answer, and there is no second page to correct it. On our side the same shift helps: AI-assisted analysis of brand mentions and online feedback classifies sentiment across languages far faster than a human team, which makes early detection realistic rather than aspirational. The optimization work itself stays human.

questions.title: How do you measure brand reputation?
questions.answer: Against a baseline set during the audit. The standing KPIs are share of positive and neutral results on page one, share of voice against named competitors, sentiment analysis across monitored online mentions, review ratings and volume by platform, and the accuracy of AI answers about your company. Brand mention monitoring runs continuously underneath all of it, so every number has a movement behind it rather than a snapshot.

questions.title: Do you guarantee specific rankings, removals or ratings?
questions.answer: No. We commit to compliant methods and transparent reporting on what moved and what didn't, not guaranteed removals, fake reviews or blackhat tactics.

questions.title: Is this the same as PR, and can you work alongside our in-house team?
questions.answer: It is not the same, and yes. Public relations shapes what publications say about you; this shapes what anyone finds afterwards, which includes coverage but also review platforms, forums, AI answers and your own online brand assets. Digital marketing drives demand; this work makes sure the person that demand sends to Google finds a positive reputation waiting. RH Control is built to run alongside in-house marketing, PR, communications and compliance teams as operational capacity, not as a replacement for the function.

questions.title: Which industries and regions do you cover?
questions.answer: Most of our work is reputation management for fintech companies, SaaS and B2B technology vendors, healthcare and pharma, e-commerce brands, automotive, FMCG, professional firms, real estate, legal practices, retail brands, senior living operators, hospitality groups, educational institutions, construction firms, restaurant groups and cryptocurrency companies, including public companies and private businesses with a public profile.

questions.title: What should you look for in a reputation management company?
questions.answer: Three things separate a reputation management agency worth retaining from one that is not. First, method transparency: a reputation management firm that names what it will actually do, and refuses fake reviews and blackhat SEO in writing. Second, coverage: whether it can act on search, reviews, media and AI answers, or only on one of them. Third, accountability: a named strategist, agreed KPIs and reporting tied to business outcomes rather than impressions. Ranking lists of the best reputation management companies are a starting point, not an answer, since almost none of them disclose method.

questions.title: Is the work confidential?
questions.answer: Yes. Every engagement runs under strict confidentiality terms, designed to be discreet by default, including work involving named executives.
